a: A hotel front desk handing every arriving guest a room number, a map, and a checkout time.
e: DHCP hands out IP settings; a rogue DHCP server can redirect a whole network.

a: A small note taped inside the browser telling it which side door to use for each address.
e: A PAC file only picks a proxy per URL; it encrypts nothing itself.

a: A screen door on a bank vault — it looks like a lock, but anyone can push through in minutes.
e: WEP's reused IVs make it crackable in minutes; never deploy it.

a: A quick patch on WEP's broken lock while the proper door was still being built.
e: WPA used TKIP as a stopgap; WPA2 brought proper AES encryption.

a: A solid deadbolt for Wi-Fi — strong, unless the shared password is weak enough to guess.
e: WPA2-Personal falls to offline password guessing; WPA3's SAE fixes that.

a: A spare key hidden under the doormat with only an eight-digit lock on the box.
e: WPS PINs are checked in two halves, so brute force takes only hours; disable it.

a: Registered mail: numbered, signed for, and resent if it gets lost.
e: TCP guarantees ordered delivery through a 3-way handshake; UDP skips all that.

a: Shouting announcements across a stadium — fast, but nobody confirms they heard you.
e: UDP has no handshake or retransmission, ideal for DNS, VoIP and streaming.

a: The internet's phone book, turning names you remember into numbers machines dial.
e: Plain DNS is unauthenticated, which is why poisoning works and DNSSEC exists.

a: Handing a box through the secure SSH tunnel instead of throwing it over the fence.
e: SCP copies files over SSH but, unlike SFTP, cannot browse or resume.

a: The old dial-up back door into the office network, from before VPNs became standard.
e: RAS is the legacy dial-in concept; VPNs replaced it with encrypted internet tunnels.

a: Building a secure tunnel to the gatekeeper first, then whispering your password inside it.
e: EAP-TTLS needs only a server certificate, unlike EAP-TLS which needs client certificates too.

a: A tunnel built from cardboard: still standing, but it collapses the moment anyone pushes.
e: PPTP's MS-CHAPv2 authentication is broken; replace it with IPSec or TLS VPNs.

a: Shouting names down an old office corridor to find colleagues — chatty and easy to eavesdrop on.
e: NetBIOS leaks host and share information; disable it where not needed.
m: Network eavesdroppers Track Broadcasts In Old Systems

a: Calling a coworker and asking them to run a task on their desk as if it were yours.
e: RPC lets programs call code remotely, a frequent lateral movement path.

a: A restaurant menu and waiter: you order through the counter, never walking into the kitchen.
e: An API exposes functions to other programs, so it needs authentication and rate limits.

a: The network's radar ping and error notes — 'are you there?' and 'can't get there from here'.
e: ICMP powers ping and traceroute but can be abused for floods and reconnaissance.

a: A company switchboard: outsiders see one main number, never the extensions behind it.
e: NAT conserves IPv4 addresses and hides internal hosts, but it is not a firewall.

a: One apartment building address, with each resident's mail sorted by apartment number.
e: PAT tracks sessions by port number so many hosts share one public IP.

a: A full file-cabinet service delivered through the SSH tunnel — browse, upload, rename, resume.
e: SFTP is an SSH subsystem on port 22, unrelated to FTP despite the name.

a: Mailing your files and your password on postcards for every mail carrier to read.
e: FTP on 20/21 sends credentials in cleartext; replace it with SFTP or FTPS.

a: The same old FTP postcards, now sealed in TLS envelopes.
e: FTPS is FTP over TLS with separate data channels; SFTP is a different, SSH-based protocol.

a: The internet's postal agreements between countries — whoever announces a route is mostly trusted.
e: BGP trusts route announcements, so hijacks can reroute whole networks' traffic.

a: An empty armored-truck chassis: it carries cargo, but you must add IPSec for the armor.
e: L2TP only tunnels; security comes entirely from pairing it with IPSec.

a: The same mail trucks between post offices, now with the cargo locked in TLS boxes.
e: SMTPS encrypts mail between hops, typically implicit TLS on port 465.

a: The town clock everyone sets their watch by — if it's wrong, logs and Kerberos tickets break.
e: Accurate time keeps logs correlatable and Kerberos working within its five-minute skew.

a: A building manager's clipboard checking every thermostat and meter remotely — old versions leave the clipboard on the lobby counter.
e: SNMPv1 and v2c use cleartext community strings; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption.

a: The courier service for old internet bulletin boards called Usenet newsgroups.
e: NNTP on port 119 carries Usenet articles; it is largely legacy today.

a: A loading dock with no ID check, used to drop boot files onto devices quickly.
e: TFTP has no authentication at all; keep it on isolated management networks.

a: A hotel of remote desktops, where many users check into their own sessions on one server.
e: RDS is the Windows service hosting sessions; RDP is the protocol carrying them.

a: Sending a formal letter in a strict XML envelope with every field filled out.
e: SOAP is a rigid XML standard with built-in WS-Security, unlike lightweight REST.

a: Calling a taxi when you need a ride, instead of keeping a private driver on salary.
e: An SVC is built per session; a PVC stays permanently provisioned.

a: The control room of a refinery, coordinating thousands of valves and sensors across the plant.
e: A DCS controls one plant locally; SCADA supervises assets spread over wide areas.

a: The catalog of every gauge and dial a managed device exposes to SNMP.
e: The MIB defines what can be read; OIDs address individual entries.

a: The building manager's central dashboard watching every device's vital signs.
e: The NMS is the manager; SNMP agents on devices answer its queries.

a: The receptionist who dials, connects, and hangs up calls but never carries the conversation itself.
e: SIP only signals calls; the voice itself travels separately, usually over RTP.

a: A Dewey Decimal number pointing to exactly one book in the SNMP library.
e: An OID is just an address; the MIB defines what lives there.

a: The customs rulebook deciding which packages get sealed, waved through, or rejected.
e: The SPD decides what to protect; IKE negotiates how to protect it.

a: A universal ID checkpoint that accepts passports, badges or fingerprints — whichever method you plug in.
e: EAP is a framework, not a method; EAP-TLS and EAP-TTLS are methods inside it.

a: A tamper-evident wax seal on outgoing mail, verifiable with a public stamp published in DNS.
e: DKIM signs the message itself; SPF only checks which server sent it.

a: A guest list published by your domain naming which mail servers may send on its behalf.
e: SPF validates the sending server's IP; it says nothing about message tampering.

a: The rulebook telling mail servers what to do with a letter that fails the seal and guest-list checks.
e: DMARC tells receivers to quarantine or reject failures and sends reports back.

a: The apartment number on an envelope inside the building — it only matters on the local hallway.
e: A destination MAC only gets a frame across one local hop, then gets rewritten.

a: A tamper seal on a transparent envelope — proves nothing changed, but anyone can read it.
e: AH authenticates packets but does not encrypt, and it breaks through NAT.

a: A sealed, opaque, tamper-evident envelope for every packet.
e: ESP encrypts and authenticates, which is why it is used far more than AH.

a: A ready-made blacklist of known tricks that a WAF bouncer memorizes before the shift.
e: CRS is the rule set; the WAF is the engine that enforces it.

a: A customs office for outbound traffic, checking where employees browse and what they download.
e: A SWG protects users going out; a WAF protects apps coming in.

a: A burglar who moves into your attic for months, quietly learning the house before stealing anything.
e: APTs are patient, resourced and targeted, often nation-state backed.

a: Hiring a thousand people to stand in a shop doorway so real customers can't get in.
e: DDoS attacks availability from many sources at once, unlike a single-source DoS.

a: A mail carrier who opens, reads, and reseals every letter before delivering it.
e: MITM breaks confidentiality and integrity; TLS with proper certificate validation defeats it.
